name: GRATERS OF THE SAUCED HAVART (i) BURGER

recipe.history:
Havarti is Denmark's most beloved cheese, a semi-soft, washed-curd cow's milk cheese that was developed in the mid-19th century by Hanne Nielsen, a pioneering Danish cheesemaker and farmer who traveled across Europe studying cheese-making traditions before returning to her farm — named Havarthigaard — in the hills north of Copenhagen to develop her own style. Her innovation was a washed-curd process in which the curds are rinsed in warm water during production, reducing acidity and producing a milder, more buttery flavor than aged washed-rind cheeses, and a smooth, supple, slightly springy texture dotted with small irregular holes from the fermentation process. Named for her farm, Havarti became a staple of the Danish dairy industry, produced in plain form and in varieties flavored with dill, caraway, jalapeño, and cream. The cream Havarti, enriched with additional cream during production, is particularly prized for its exceptional melt — it flows smoothly into a liquid pool over heat with none of the greasiness that afflicts lower-quality melting cheeses — making it one of the finest burger cheeses in existence.

Havarti entered the American cheese lexicon through Danish and Scandinavian immigrant communities in the Midwest, particularly in Wisconsin and Minnesota, where Scandinavian dairy traditions found fertile ground in the American cheese-making industry. By the latter half of the 20th century, American-produced Havarti had become a deli case staple, prized for its mild buttery flavor and excellent meltability. Its transition to burgers was a natural evolution of its use in hot sandwiches and melts, and the cheese's neutral buttery quality — not as sharp as cheddar, not as pungent as Swiss, not as elastic as mozzarella — made it an ideal canvas for building burger flavor profiles that featured bold sauces and toppings without the cheese competing for attention. Grated Havarti, in particular, melts faster and more evenly than sliced, creating a uniform, glossy, creamy cap over the entire surface of the patty.

I keep a block of cream Havarti in my refrigerator with the same reliability that I keep butter and eggs — it is a foundational ingredient, not a specialty item. I started grating it over burgers rather than slicing it after noticing that slices melted unevenly and left patches of unmelted cheese at the edges. Grating the Havarti and mounding it over the hot patty produces a complete, even melt in about ninety seconds, and the resulting cheese cap is smooth, glossy, and deeply creamy in a way that a slice never quite achieves. The 'sauced' in the burger name refers to a bold, mustardy cream sauce that plays to Havarti's Danish heritage, and together the sauce and the grated melted cheese create a double-cream richness that demands nothing less than a properly medium rare patty to balance it.

There is a particular pleasure in the combination of a great melting cheese and a properly medium rare beef patty that I cannot fully explain except to say that the pleasure depends entirely on the beef being cooked correctly. Havarti melts into the hot surface of a seared patty and the cheese's fat and the beef's fat mingle in a way that is physically and culinarily beautiful — but only if the beef is at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 Celsius. At higher temperatures, the beef's fat has already rendered away and the cheese sits on a dry surface with nothing to bond to; the two fats never truly combine. At medium rare, the beef's rendered intramuscular fat is still present and warm and the Havarti dissolves directly into it. The cheese becomes part of the patty. Cook to medium rare. Grate the Havarti. Watch them become one.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
250g cream Havarti cheese, coarsely grated on the large holes of a box grater
salt and white pepper to taste
1/2 cup crispy shallots (thinly sliced shallots fried in oil until golden)
instructions: 1. Make the mustard cream sauce: Melt butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add shallot and garlic and cook 3 to 4 minutes until softened. Add white wine and cook until reduced by half, about 3 minutes. Add heavy cream and simmer until reduced and thickened slightly, about 4 minutes. Remove from heat and whisk in whole grain mustard, Dijon, thyme, and lemon juice. Season with salt and white pepper. Keep warm over very low heat.

2. Make the crispy shallots: Slice 3 large shallots into thin rings. Toss in a small bowl with 2 tbsp all-purpose flour and a pinch of salt until lightly coated. Heat 1/4 inch of neutral oil in a small skillet over medium-high heat. Fry shallots in batches for 2 to 3 minutes until deep golden brown. Drain on paper towels and season immediately with salt. They will crisp further as they cool.

3. Cook the bacon: In a cold skillet, lay bacon strips flat. Heat over medium, turning occasionally, until crispy and deeply browned, about 8 to 10 minutes. Transfer to paper towels. Reserve skillet fat.

4. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead with dough hook on medium for 8 minutes until smooth. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 equal portions, shape into smooth balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash, sprinkle sesame seeds, and bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.
5. Grate the Havarti: On the large holes of a box grater, coarsely grate the cream Havarti into a bowl. Set aside at room temperature.

6. Shape the patties: Season ground beef with salt, black pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 4 equal portions and shape into patties 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than the buns. Press a dimple into the center of each.
7. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties undisturbed for 3 minutes.

8. Flip patties. Immediately mound a generous pile of grated Havarti over each patty. Add a splash of water to the skillet and cover briefly with a lid or foil to create steam and melt the cheese completely, about 60 to 90 seconds. Check temperature — remove patties at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Tent loosely with foil and rest 3 to 4 minutes.
9. Toast buns cut-side down in residual bacon fat and skillet fat for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

10. Assemble: Spoon mustard cream sauce generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place butter lettuce on the bottom bun, followed by tomato slices and two strips of bacon. Set the patty with its fully melted Havarti cap on top. Drizzle additional mustard cream sauce over the cheese. Top with crispy shallots. Close the bun and serve immediately.
